title: Automate Anything with Make
description: Build visual no-code automations with Make: scenarios, modules, routers, filters, and AI integrations, plus an honest comparison with n8n and Zapier.

lessons.title: Make in One Sentence
lessons.bodyMd:
## Make in one sentence

Make is a visual automation platform where you build workflows by connecting app icons on a canvas. A new email arrives, Make catches it, summarizes it with AI, logs it in a spreadsheet, and notifies your team in Slack. All without writing code.

It started life as Integromat, a Czech company founded in 2016. Celonis acquired it, and it was rebranded as Make. The Integromat DNA still shows: this is a tool built by automation nerds, and it is far more powerful than its friendly interface suggests.

## What does it actually do?

Make connects thousands of apps and services and moves data between them on triggers you define. The unit of automation in Make is called a **scenario**. A scenario is one complete workflow, like "when a form is submitted, enrich the lead, add it to my CRM, and send a welcome email."

Every scenario has a flow that reads left to right on the canvas:

1. A **trigger** watches for an event (a new row in a sheet, a form submission, a scheduled time).
2. **Modules** perform actions (send an email, create a database record, call an AI model).
3. The data flows from module to module as **bundles**, little packages of fields you can map into the next step.

## Why people choose Make

Three things keep coming up when teams pick Make over alternatives:

**The visual canvas.** Every scenario is a flowchart you can see, zoom, and rearrange. Debugging a 20 step automation in Make feels like reading a map. In text based tools it feels like reading a log file.

**Serious logic, no code.** Routers split one flow into branches. Filters decide which branch runs. Iterators loop through lists. Aggregators combine results back together. These are real programming concepts, but you build them by clicking, not by typing syntax.

**The pricing model.** Make charges by **operations**, meaning each module that runs in a scenario counts as one operation. The free tier gives you a meaningful monthly allowance to learn and run real workflows, and paid tiers scale with usage rather than per seat. That makes it unusually affordable for small teams.

## Who is it for?

Make fits people who want more than the simple "when this happens, do that" style of basic automation tools, but who do not want to write and maintain code. Marketers routing leads, founders building AI pipelines, operations people syncing tools, freelancers delivering client automations. If you can think in flowcharts, you can build in Make.

## What you will build in this guide

By chapter 5 you will have built working scenarios, understood routers and filters, wired AI into your automations, and you will know exactly how Make compares to n8n and Zapier so you can pick the right tool with confidence. Let us start with the vocabulary.

lessons.title: The Vocabulary: Scenarios, Modules, and Operations
lessons.bodyMd:
## The six words you need

Make has its own vocabulary. Learn these six terms and everything else clicks into place.

## 1. Scenario

A scenario is one complete automation, start to finish. "Watch my Gmail for invoices, extract the totals, and log them in a spreadsheet" is one scenario. Think of it as a recipe: the scenario is the whole recipe, not one ingredient.

## 2. Module

A module is a single step inside a scenario. Each module represents one app doing one thing: "Send an email," "Create a Notion page," "Call the OpenAI API." Modules appear as circles on the canvas, connected by lines showing the data flow.

## 3. Trigger

The trigger is the first module in every scenario. It defines what starts the workflow. Triggers come in a few flavors:

- **Watch events (polling):** Make checks the app on a schedule, like every 15 minutes, for new items. "Watch for new rows in Google Sheets" is a polling trigger.
- **Instant triggers (webhooks):** The app tells Make immediately when something happens. Faster, but not every app supports them.
- **Scheduled:** The scenario simply runs at a time you set, like every morning at 8 AM.

## 4. Bundle

A bundle is the package of data that travels between modules. When your trigger fires, it produces a bundle containing all the fields from that event: the email subject, the sender, the body. Each following module receives the bundle, uses what it needs, and passes its own results onward.

## 5. Operation

An operation is Make's billing unit. Roughly, one operation equals one module running one time. If your scenario has 5 modules and runs once, that is 5 operations. This matters for pricing, so keep it in mind: a scenario that polls every 15 minutes and checks 10 modules each time burns operations fast, even when nothing changed.

## 6. Connection

A connection is Make's saved login to an app. The first time you add a Gmail module, you authorize Make to access your Gmail, and Make stores that connection. After that, every Gmail module in every scenario can reuse it. Connections are the reason building your second scenario is so much faster than your first.

## How it feels in practice

Here is a concrete example. You build a scenario called "Save email attachments."

1. Trigger: Gmail "Watch emails" with a filter for emails with attachments.
2. Module: Google Drive "Upload a file," mapping the attachment from the bundle.
3. Module: Slack "Send a message" to your team channel: "New attachment saved: [filename]."

Three modules, one scenario, zero code. The mapping step is the core skill of Make: you click into a field and pick which piece of data from a previous module goes there. Once you are comfortable with mapping, you can build almost anything.

lessons.title: What Make Is Great At (and Where It Struggles)
lessons.bodyMd:
## Why Make exists

Before tools like Make, connecting two apps meant one of three things: pay a developer, use a rigid one trick integration, or copy paste data by hand. For a freelancer that meant hours of admin. For a small business it meant the tools never quite talked to each other.

Make's bet is that visual workflows can replace a surprising amount of custom code. And for a huge class of problems, they are right.

## What Make is genuinely great at

**App plumbing.** Moving data between the tools you already use. New Shopify order to QuickBooks to Slack notification. Form submission to CRM to personalized follow up email. This is the bread and butter, and Make handles it with more flexibility than simpler tools because you can transform and branch the data mid flow.

**Multi step processes.** Because one scenario can hold unlimited modules with branches, loops, and error handling, you can model real business processes: an onboarding flow with five branches depending on customer type, a content pipeline that researches, drafts, reviews, and publishes.

**AI pipelines.** Make has native modules for OpenAI, Anthropic, and other AI providers. That turns it into a visual way to build AI workflows: scrape a page, ask AI to summarize it, store the summary, send it to the team. You get the AI power without building a backend.

**Prototyping fast.** Need to test whether an automation idea is worth building properly? A Make scenario takes an afternoon, not a sprint. Many production workflows at real companies started as "temporary" Make scenarios that never needed replacing.

## Where Make struggles

Honest limits, so you go in with eyes open:

**Polling eats operations.** Many triggers check for new data on a schedule, and every check costs operations whether or not anything changed. A scenario polling every minute with no results still burns through your allowance. Use webhooks where available, and set sensible intervals.

**Complex logic gets visually messy.** A scenario with eight branches and nested routers is powerful but hard to read six months later. Discipline helps: name your modules, add notes to the canvas, split giant scenarios into smaller ones that call each other.

**It is still a third party in the middle.** If Make has an outage, your automations pause. For truly mission critical, millisecond sensitive systems, code you own may be safer. For everything else, the tradeoff is usually worth it.

## The bottom line

Make is the sweet spot between "too simple to be useful" and "requires an engineering team." You do not need to love it for everything. You need to know what it is for: connecting apps, moving data, and adding AI to your processes, all on a canvas you can actually see and debug.

lessons.title: Building Your First Scenario Step by Step
lessons.bodyMd:
## What you need before you start

An account at make.com (the free tier is enough for everything in this guide), plus accounts in two apps we will connect: Gmail and Google Sheets. You will authorize Make to access them, which takes about a minute per app.

## Step 1: Create your first scenario

Log in and click **Create a new scenario**. You get a blank canvas with a big plus button in the middle. That plus is where your trigger goes. Everything in Make starts by answering one question: what kicks this off?

## Step 2: Add your trigger

Click the plus and search for Gmail. Choose the **Watch emails** module. This is a polling trigger: it will check your inbox on a schedule for new messages.

Configure it:

- **Connection:** Click Add, sign in with Google, and grant Make access. This creates a reusable connection.
- **Folder:** Select INBOX.
- **Filter type:** Choose "Simple" and set a filter you can test safely, like emails with a specific label. Create a Gmail label called `make-test` and filter on that, so you control exactly when it fires.
- **Maximum number of results:** Set this to 1 while testing, so each run handles a single email.

Click OK. Your trigger module is now sitting on the canvas.

## Step 3: Add an action module

Click the plus after the Gmail module and search for Google Sheets. Choose **Add a row**. Select your connection (or create one), pick a spreadsheet and sheet, and map the fields: email subject to column A, sender to column B, date to column C. Mapping is the click and pick step: click a field, choose the bundle item from the previous module.

## Step 4: Run it once

At the bottom of the canvas, click **Run once**. Make executes the scenario immediately. Send yourself an email with the `make-test` label first, so there is data to process. Watch the modules light up as the bundle flows through. Click any module after the run to inspect exactly what data went in and what came out. This inspection view is your best debugging friend.

## Step 5: Set the schedule and switch it on

Click the clock icon on the trigger to set how often it polls. Every 15 minutes is a good default. Then flip the scenario switch to ON. It now runs on its own, around the clock.

You just built a real automation: labeled emails land in a spreadsheet automatically. Simple, but every scenario you ever build follows this same skeleton: trigger, modules, mapping, test, schedule, activate.

lessons.title: Connections, Webhooks, and the HTTP Module
lessons.bodyMd:
## Connections are the foundation

A connection is a saved authorization between Make and one of your apps. You create it once, and every scenario can reuse it. This is worth understanding well, because connection problems cause a large share of beginner frustration.

## Creating a connection

When you add a module for an app you have not connected yet, Make prompts you to create a connection. Usually this means an OAuth sign in: Make opens the app's login page, you approve access, and Make stores a token. Some apps need an API key instead, which you paste from the app's settings page.

Give connections clear names, especially if you manage multiple accounts. "Gmail, work" and "Gmail, personal" will save you from sending client emails from the wrong address.

## Scopes and permissions

When you authorize, the app tells you what Make can do: read emails, send emails, manage spreadsheets. Only grant what the automation needs. If a scenario only reads a sheet, do not grant write access. This is basic hygiene, and it limits damage if a token ever leaks.

## Reauthorizing

Tokens expire. Apps change their APIs. When a module suddenly fails with an authorization error after working for months, the fix is almost always to reauthorize the connection: open the connection settings, click reauthorize, sign in again. Do not rebuild the scenario. The scenario is fine; the token just went stale.

## Webhooks: the faster trigger

Some triggers work by polling: Make asks the app "anything new?" on a schedule. Others use webhooks: the app calls Make the instant something happens. Webhooks are faster and cheaper in operations, because there are no empty checks.

To use one, add a **Custom webhook** module as your trigger. Make gives you a unique URL. Paste that URL into the app's webhook settings (in the app's own dashboard, outside Make). Now every event in that app fires your scenario instantly. Use webhooks whenever the app supports them, especially for high volume scenarios.

## The HTTP module: the universal adapter

What if the app you need has no Make module? The **HTTP** module lets you call any API directly. You provide the URL, method, headers, and body, just like a developer would, but inside the visual canvas. Combined with the **Parse JSON** tool, the HTTP module means Make can talk to essentially any modern service. If you can read an API doc, you can integrate anything.

lessons.title: Testing, Debugging, and Error Handling
lessons.bodyMd:
## Always test with "Run once"

Before you switch any scenario on, click **Run once** at the bottom of the canvas. This executes the scenario immediately with real data, and you can watch each module process its bundle. Make highlights the path the data took, so you can see exactly which branches ran.

After a run, click any module to open its execution detail. You see the input bundle (what came in) and the output bundle (what went out). When something looks wrong, this is where you find out why. Ninety percent of debugging in Make is staring at bundles until the mismatch jumps out.

## The scenario log

Every execution is recorded in the scenario's history. Open a scenario, click the history tab, and you see each run: when it ran, whether it succeeded, and how many operations it used. Failed runs show the error message from the module that broke. This log is how you discover that your scenario has been failing quietly at 2 AM for a week.

## Common failures and fixes

**"The operation failed with an error."** Read the actual error text in the module detail. API errors usually name the problem: a missing required field, an invalid date format, a permission issue. Fix the mapping, not the module.

**"Bundle incomplete" or missing data.** Your trigger produced a bundle without the field you mapped. This happens when the test data differs from real data. Run once with realistic data, not a perfect sample.

**Scenario runs but does nothing.** Check your filters. A filter that is too strict silently drops every bundle. Temporarily remove filters, run once, confirm data flows, then re add them.

**It worked yesterday and broke today.** Almost always a stale connection or a changed field in the source app. Reauthorize first, then check whether the app renamed or removed a field you mapped.

## Error handling basics

Make lets you define what happens when a module fails. Right click a module and add an **error handler** route: a separate path that runs only on failure. Common patterns: send yourself a Slack alert with the error text, write the failed bundle to a spreadsheet for manual review, or use the **Ignore** directive to skip the error and continue.

You will go deeper on routers and filters in the next chapter. For now, remember the workflow: run once, inspect bundles, check the log, fix the mapping.

lessons.title: Triggers, Actions, and Tool Modules
lessons.bodyMd:
## Triggers start it, actions do the work

Every scenario begins with exactly one trigger module. Everything after it is an action, a search, or a tool. Understanding what each module type is for will make building feel obvious.

## Trigger modules

Triggers watch for something and start the scenario. The icon has a little lightning bolt. Examples: Gmail "Watch emails," Google Sheets "Watch new rows," Webhook "Custom webhook," or the built in **Schedule** trigger that simply runs at times you set.

Two behaviors to know:

- **Polling triggers** check on an interval. You set the schedule, and Make looks for new items each time. Simple and universal, but each check costs operations.
- **Instant triggers** fire the moment the event happens, via webhook. Faster and cheaper, but only some apps support them.

## Action modules

Actions do something in an app: send an email, create a record, post a message, update a row. They take the incoming bundle, do their job, and pass results onward.

## Search and get modules

These read data without changing anything: "Search records" in Airtable, "Get a file" in Drive, "List messages" in Slack. Use them to look things up mid scenario, like finding the customer record that matches an incoming email address.

## Tools: Make's built in utilities

The **Tools** section holds modules that are not tied to any app. The ones you will use constantly:

- **Set variable:** Store a value to reuse later in the scenario.
- **Get variable:** Retrieve it.
- **Text parser:** Extract patterns from text with regular expressions or simple matching.
- **Date and time:** Format dates, calculate differences, convert time zones.
- **JSON:** Parse a JSON string into mappable fields, or build JSON from fields.
- **Math:** Do calculations on numbers from your bundles.

## A practical pattern: lookup then act

A very common scenario shape is: trigger fires, search module looks up related data, action module uses both. Example: a new support email arrives (trigger), you search your CRM for the sender (search), then you reply with their plan details included (action). The search module enriches the bundle, and the action gets smarter. Master this pattern and you can build genuinely useful automations, not just notifications.

## Scheduling strategies

The schedule you put on a trigger is a design decision, not an afterthought. Polling every minute gives you near real time results but burns operations on empty checks. Polling once a day is cheap but slow. Match the interval to the stakes: order notifications deserve 15 minutes, a weekly report deserves a weekly schedule.

A useful trick is the **two scenario pattern**: a lightweight watcher scenario that polls frequently and does almost nothing, which then triggers a heavy worker scenario via webhook only when there is real work. The watcher costs a few operations per check; the worker's expensive AI calls and multi step logic only run when needed.

## Watching the right thing

Polling triggers usually let you choose what counts as "new": new rows, new or updated rows, or items matching a filter. Choosing narrowly saves operations and prevents duplicate processing. If your sheet gets rows added and edited, "watch new rows" avoids reprocessing every edit. Think about what your scenario actually needs to react to, and configure the trigger to watch exactly that.

lessons.title: Routers: Branching Your Scenarios
lessons.bodyMd:
## One flow becomes many

A **router** splits a scenario into multiple paths. Data arrives at the router, and Make sends it down one or more branches based on rules you define. This is how you build "if this, do that; otherwise do something else" logic visually.

## Adding a router

Click the plus between two modules and choose **Router** from the tools. The router appears as a junction, and you can attach multiple branches to it. Each branch gets its own chain of modules.

## Filters decide which branch runs

A **filter** sits on the line between the router and a branch. It is a condition like "email subject contains the word invoice" or "deal value is greater than 1000." When a bundle reaches the router, Make checks each branch's filter. The bundle flows down every branch whose filter passes.

This "every matching branch" behavior surprises beginners. If two filters both pass, the bundle goes down both branches. That is a feature: one event can trigger a Slack notification AND a spreadsheet log AND a CRM update in parallel.

## Fallback routes

What if no filter matches? Add a branch with no filter, or with a filter that catches everything else. Make evaluates branches in order, so put your specific filters first and the catch all last. The catch all branch handles the unexpected: log it, alert someone, or just ignore it deliberately.

## Real example: lead routing

A form submission arrives via webhook. The router splits three ways:

- **Branch 1**, filter: company size greater than 200. Modules: create a Salesforce opportunity, assign to the enterprise rep, send a Slack alert to the sales channel.
- **Branch 2**, filter: company size between 20 and 200. Modules: add to HubSpot, enroll in the mid market email sequence.
- **Branch 3**, no filter (fallback). Modules: add to the newsletter list, send a thank you email.

One scenario, three different customer journeys, all visible on one canvas. Try building that with simple "if this then that" rules and you will feel the difference.

## Tips for readable routers

Name every branch by clicking its label: "Enterprise," "Mid market," "Fallback." Add notes to the canvas explaining the business rule. And resist the urge to nest routers five deep. If a branch needs complex logic of its own, split it into a separate scenario and call it with the **Run a scenario** module or a webhook.

lessons.title: Filters, Iterators, and Aggregators
lessons.bodyMd:
## Filters are the gatekeepers

You met filters on router branches. They also work on any connection between any two modules. A filter between module A and module B means: only continue to B if this condition is true. It is the simplest way to add "only if" logic anywhere in a scenario.

Filter conditions compare a field from the bundle against a value: equals, contains, greater than, exists, and more. You can combine conditions with AND and OR. Example: continue only if the email is from a customer AND the subject contains "urgent."

## Iterators: one bundle becomes many

Sometimes a module outputs a list inside a single bundle: an order with ten line items, a form with five file uploads, a search that returned twenty records. An **iterator** splits that list so each item becomes its own bundle, and every module after the iterator runs once per item.

Example: Gmail finds an email with 5 attachments. The iterator splits them. The Google Drive upload module after it runs 5 times, once per attachment. Without the iterator, you would only process the first one.

## Aggregators: many bundles become one

An **aggregator** does the reverse: it collects multiple bundles back into one. After an iterator processes ten items, an aggregator can combine the results into a single summary bundle.

The classic pair is **Text aggregator**: collect all ten processed items into one block of text, then send a single email containing all of them instead of ten separate emails. Other aggregators build arrays, tables, or archives (like zipping files).

## Putting it together: the digest pattern

This iterator plus aggregator pattern is one of the most useful in all of Make:

1. Trigger: schedule, every morning at 7 AM.
2. Search: find all new support tickets from the last 24 hours (one bundle containing a list).
3. Iterator: split into one bundle per ticket.
4. AI module: summarize each ticket in one sentence.
5. Text aggregator: combine all summaries into one digest.
6. Action: send one Slack message with the full digest.

Without the iterator, the AI sees one giant blob. Without the aggregator, the team gets spammed with twenty messages. Together they turn a list into a clean daily briefing. Learn this pattern and you will reuse it constantly.

## When to use which

Beginners often reach for a router when a filter would do, or an aggregator when nothing needs combining. A quick rule of thumb:

- One condition, one path: a **filter** on the connection line is enough.
- One event, several different responses: a **router** with branches.
- A list that needs item by item work: an **iterator** before the work.
- Item by item results that should become one message or file: an **aggregator** after the work.

## Nested iterators: handle with care

Sometimes you need an iterator inside an iterator: an email with attachments where each attachment needs multiple processing steps. This works, but operations multiply fast. Ten emails times five attachments times three steps is 150 operations per run. Before building nested loops, ask whether the inner work can be simplified or whether a filter can skip items that do not need processing. Loops are the number one cause of surprise operation bills.

## Aggregator types worth knowing

Beyond the text aggregator, two others come up constantly. The **array aggregator** collects bundles into a structured list you can map into APIs that expect arrays. The **table aggregator** builds rows you can write to a spreadsheet in one action instead of one row per bundle. Choosing the right aggregator is often the difference between a scenario that sends fifty emails and one that sends a single clean report.

lessons.title: Adding AI to Any Scenario
lessons.bodyMd:
## AI as a module, not a separate tool

Make has native modules for major AI providers, including OpenAI and Anthropic. That means AI becomes just another module in your scenario: data flows in, a prompt runs, the result flows out to the next module. You do not need a separate AI subscription for the automation logic; you connect your AI provider account and pay for usage through it.

## The basic AI pattern

The simplest AI module setup looks like this:

1. Some trigger produces text: a new email, a form response, a scraped page.
2. An AI module receives the text inside a prompt you write, for example: "Summarize the following customer message in one sentence and classify it as praise, complaint, or question: [message text]."
3. The next module uses the AI's output: the classification routes the ticket, the summary goes into a digest.

The square brackets are mapping: you insert the bundle field into your prompt template. The prompt is fixed text you write once; the data changes every run.

## Prompt design for automations

Prompts inside scenarios need to be more rigid than prompts you type into a chat app. An automation cannot ask follow up questions, so tell the model exactly what shape you want back.

Good automation prompts do three things:

- **Constrain the output format.** "Reply with exactly one word: praise, complaint, or question." Structured output makes the next module's filter trivial to write.
- **Give a role and context.** "You are a support triage assistant for a software company." Two sentences of context beat a clever prompt with none.
- **Show an example.** "Example input: 'Your app crashed again.' Example output: complaint." One example often fixes inconsistent results.

## A real example: smart email triage

Scenario: Gmail trigger watches for new emails. An AI module classifies each one and drafts a reply. A router splits three ways based on the classification: complaints go to the support lead with the draft attached for review, questions get an auto reply from a template enriched with the AI draft, praise gets forwarded to the marketing folder. Human review sits on the sensitive branch; full automation on the safe ones.

## Cost awareness

AI modules consume your AI provider's usage, not just Make operations. A scenario that summarizes a hundred long emails a day can generate a real API bill. Start with smaller, cheaper models for classification and extraction tasks, and reserve the big models for work that needs genuine reasoning. You will learn more about model selection in the AI tools section of the academy.

lessons.title: Building AI Agents in Make
lessons.bodyMd:
## From pipelines to agents

Everything so far has been linear: data flows through fixed steps. Make also supports **AI agents**: modules that can reason, choose tools, and loop until a task is done, rather than following a fixed path.

## What a Make AI agent does

You give the agent a goal in plain language and a set of tools (which are just Make modules or app actions it is allowed to use). The agent then works toward the goal: it might search your calendar, check your inbox, draft a message, and ask you a clarifying question, deciding each step itself.

Example: "Prepare my briefing for tomorrow." The agent checks your calendar for tomorrow's events, looks up the attendees in your CRM, searches recent emails with each attendee, and compiles a briefing doc. The steps are not pre wired. The agent figures them out.

## When agents beat fixed scenarios

Use a fixed scenario when the process is predictable: every invoice follows the same steps. Use an agent when the process needs judgment: researching a topic, triaging ambiguous requests, or handling tasks where the right steps depend on what is discovered along the way.

## Building your first agent

In Make, agent functionality is available through AI agent modules and features. The pattern:

1. Define the goal clearly in the agent's instructions. Vague goals produce vague behavior.
2. Give it the minimum tools it needs. An agent with twenty tools gets confused; an agent with four well chosen tools stays focused.
3. Set boundaries. Tell it what it must never do: never send emails without approval, never delete records, never spend money.
4. Test with the Run once button and watch its reasoning. Agents show their thinking, which makes debugging surprisingly pleasant.

## The human in the loop

The most reliable agent pattern for beginners is approval based: the agent does the research and drafting, then pauses and asks you to approve before acting. You get 90 percent of the leverage with almost none of the risk. A scenario that drafts all your follow up emails for one click approval beats a fully autonomous one that occasionally sends something regrettable.

## Designing agent instructions

An agent is only as good as its instructions. Write them like you are onboarding a smart new hire: state the goal, describe the tools available and when to use each, list the hard boundaries, and define what a finished result looks like. Example: "You are a meeting prep assistant. Use the calendar tool to find tomorrow's meetings, the CRM tool to look up attendees, and the email tool to draft (never send) a briefing. A finished briefing has one section per meeting with attendee background and suggested talking points."

## Common agent failure modes

Agents fail in predictable ways. **Tool confusion** happens when you give too many overlapping tools; the agent picks the wrong one. Fix it by reducing and renaming tools clearly. **Looping** happens when the agent retries a failing step forever; set a maximum step count so it stops and reports instead. **Overconfidence** happens when the agent acts on guessed data; require it to cite which tool result supports each claim. Each of these has a design fix, which is good news: agent reliability is mostly a design problem, not a model problem.

## Starting simple

Your first agent should do research and drafting only, with you approving everything. Your second agent can take low risk actions like logging data or sending internal notifications. Fully autonomous agents that touch customers or money come much later, after you have watched the agent behave correctly dozens of times. This ladder keeps the learning safe while the leverage compounds.

lessons.title: Five AI Automations Worth Building
lessons.bodyMd:
## Five automations worth building this week

Theory is nice; running automations are better. Here are five AI powered scenarios, ordered by difficulty, each genuinely useful.

## 1. Meeting notes to tasks (easy)

Trigger: new file in a Google Drive folder where you save meeting transcripts. AI module: extract action items as a list with owners and deadlines. Action: create tasks in your task manager, one per item. Never lose an action item again.

## 2. Content repurposer (easy)

Trigger: new post published on your blog (RSS or webhook). AI module: rewrite it as a LinkedIn post, a tweet thread, and a newsletter blurb. Aggregator: combine into one document. Action: save to a drafts folder for your review. One piece of content becomes four.

## 3. Lead researcher (medium)

Trigger: new row in a leads spreadsheet. HTTP module: fetch the company website. AI module: summarize what the company does, identify likely pain points, and draft a personalized first line for outreach. Action: write it all back to the spreadsheet. Your outreach stops sounding like a template.

## 4. Support sentiment radar (medium)

Trigger: schedule, hourly. Search: pull recent support tickets. Iterator plus AI: score each ticket's sentiment and urgency. Aggregator: build a summary of anything urgent or trending negative. Router: if urgent items exist, send a Slack alert; otherwise log quietly. You hear about fires before customers start tweeting.

## 5. Competitor watcher (advanced)

Trigger: schedule, daily. HTTP modules: fetch competitor pricing and changelog pages. AI module: compare against yesterday's snapshot stored in a Make data store, and describe what changed in plain language. Router: if meaningful changes, notify the team; if not, stay silent. Competitive intelligence on autopilot.

## The data store trick

Notice example 5 mentions a data store. Make's **data store** is a simple built in database: key value storage you can read and write from scenarios. It is perfect for remembering state between runs, like yesterday's prices, already processed IDs, or counters. When your scenario needs a memory, reach for the data store before reaching for an external database.

## How to pick your first three

Do not build all five at once. Pick the three that map to pain you feel weekly. The meeting notes automation pays off if you attend more than five meetings a week. The content repurposer pays off if you publish regularly but dread distribution. The lead researcher pays off if personalization is your bottleneck. Start with the one whose value you can feel by Friday.

## Measuring whether it worked

Automations deserve a quick before and after check. Time the manual process once before you build: how long does meeting follow up take today? After two weeks of running the scenario, time it again, including the review step. If you saved an hour a week, that is fifty hours a year from one afternoon of building. Write the number down. It makes the case for building the next one, and for getting your team to build their own.

## The maintenance reality

AI automations need occasional tune ups. Prompts drift as your business changes, websites redesign and break scrapers, APIs update. Budget thirty minutes a month per important scenario to review its recent runs. This is dramatically cheaper than doing the work manually, but it is not zero. The builders who succeed long term treat their scenarios like a garden: mostly self sustaining, with light regular tending.

lessons.title: Make vs Zapier: An Honest Comparison
lessons.bodyMd:
## The simple one

Zapier is the best known automation tool, and the one most people try first. Its model is beautifully simple: a **Zap** has one trigger and one or more actions in a fixed sequence. When this happens, do that, then that.

## Where Zapier wins

**Ease of learning.** If you have never automated anything, Zapier's guided setup gets you from zero to working faster than anything else. Each step is a form; you fill it in and move on.

**App coverage.** Zapier lists thousands of integrations, and for mainstream business apps its connectors are polished and well documented.

**Reliability and support.** It is a mature public company product with extensive docs, a huge template library, and support infrastructure.

## Where Make pulls ahead

**Visual branching.** Zapier's paths feature exists but feels bolted on compared to Make's routers, which are native to the canvas. Complex conditional logic is simply more natural in Make.

**Data transformation.** Iterators, aggregators, text parsers, and array tools are first class citizens in Make. In Zapier, equivalent work often needs extra steps, formatter hacks, or code.

**Cost.** This is the big one. Zapier charges per **task**, where a task is roughly one action step, and its tiers get expensive as volume grows. Make's operation based pricing is generally much cheaper for multi step scenarios. A 10 step scenario running 1,000 times a month is 10,000 tasks in Zapier versus 10,000 operations in Make, and Make's operation allowances per dollar stretch further. Always check current pricing pages before deciding, since both companies adjust tiers.

## The honest take

Choose Zapier if you want the gentlest possible start and your automations are mostly linear: form to spreadsheet to notification. Choose Make when your workflows need branches, loops, or data reshaping, or when Zapier's bill starts hurting. Many teams start on Zapier and graduate to Make. That is a fine path, not a failure.

## Migration: moving from Zapier to Make

If you outgrow Zapier, migration is straightforward but manual: there is no import button. Rebuild each Zap as a scenario, which is also an opportunity to improve it with routers and better error handling. Migrate your highest volume or most painful Zap first, run both in parallel for a week, then switch off the Zapier version. Most teams migrate three to five core workflows and leave the simple ones where they are. You do not have to move everything to benefit.

## Template ecosystems

Both platforms have large template libraries. Zapier's templates are excellent for standard business processes because of its sheer user base. Make's templates skew toward more complex, multi step scenarios, which makes sense given the platform's strengths. When evaluating either tool, search its template library for your exact use case. Finding a working template for "your" problem is worth more than any feature comparison.

## The switching cost myth

People overestimate how locked in they are. The concepts transfer completely: triggers, actions, mapping, filters. Rebuilding a ten step Zap in Make typically takes under an hour once you know both interfaces. The real switching cost is re authorizing connections and re testing, not re learning. So choose based on fit, not fear.

lessons.title: Make vs n8n: An Honest Comparison
lessons.bodyMd:
## The builder's choice

n8n is the open source automation platform, and the favorite of developers and technical teams. You can self host it for free, write JavaScript inside workflows, and inspect every byte of what it does.

## Where n8n wins

**Self hosting and control.** Run it on your own server and your data never touches a third party's cloud. For regulated industries or privacy sensitive work, this is decisive.

**Code when you need it.** n8n lets you drop into JavaScript or Python inside a workflow. Developers love this escape hatch: visual for the 90 percent, code for the tricky 10 percent.

**Cost at scale.** Self hosted n8n has no per operation billing. If you run millions of executions, the math strongly favors n8n.

## Where Make pulls ahead

**No infrastructure.** Make is fully managed. No servers, no updates, no 2 AM pages because your Docker container died. For non technical teams, this alone settles it.

**Faster to learn.** n8n's canvas looks similar, but its concepts (expressions, credentials management, execution modes) assume more technical comfort. Make's learning curve is gentler for beginners.

**AI features.** Make has invested heavily in AI native features like agents and AI assisted building. n8n has strong AI node support too, but Make packages it for a less technical audience.

## The honest take

Choose n8n if you have technical skills or a technical teammate, care about data sovereignty, or run high volumes where per operation pricing hurts. Choose Make if you want power without operating infrastructure, and your team is mostly non engineers.

They are not enemies. A common mature setup is Make for business team automations and n8n for engineering owned pipelines. Use the right tool per job.

## The hybrid reality

In practice, many teams end up using both. A marketing team runs Make for lead routing and content workflows because nobody on the team wants to manage servers. The engineering team runs n8n for data pipelines and internal tooling because they want code level control and data sovereignty. The tools coexist fine because they solve different jobs for different people.

## Learning transfer

Time spent learning Make is not wasted if you later move to n8n. The mental models are nearly identical: triggers start workflows, data maps between steps, routers branch logic, error handlers catch failures. n8n just adds expressions (a mini language for transforming data) and code nodes on top. Learners who start visual and go technical later often report that Make taught them to think in workflows, which made n8n click fast.

## Total cost of ownership

Do not compare sticker prices alone. Make's cost is the subscription plus your time building. n8n self hosted is free software plus server costs plus the engineering time to maintain it. For a non technical team, the engineering time does not exist, so Make wins easily. For a team with a DevOps person already on payroll, n8n's marginal cost is near zero. The honest comparison includes who does the maintaining, because that person is the real price.

lessons.title: How to Choose the Right Tool
lessons.bodyMd:
## A decision framework, not a verdict

There is no universally best automation tool. There is only the best tool for your situation. Here is how to decide.

## Ask these five questions

**1. Who builds and maintains it?** Non technical team: lean Make or Zapier. Developers available: n8n becomes attractive. Solo founder doing everything: pick whichever you will actually open, which is usually Make.

**2. How complex is the logic?** Simple linear flows: any tool works, Zapier is fastest to learn. Branches, loops, data merging: Make or n8n. Heavy custom code: n8n.

**3. What is the volume?** Low to medium volume: Make's pricing is hard to beat. Very high volume: n8n self hosted wins on cost. Spiky enterprise volume: compare all three carefully against current pricing.

**4. Where does the data live?** If compliance requires data to stay in your infrastructure, n8n self hosted is the answer. If you are fine with a managed cloud, Make and Zapier are simpler.

**5. How much AI is involved?** All three handle AI integrations now. Make's AI modules and agents are the most beginner friendly packaging. n8n gives developers the most control over AI pipelines. Gumloop, covered in the next guide, is the AI first specialist.

## A practical starting path

If you are new and unsure: start with Make's free tier. Build three real scenarios. You will learn the core concepts (triggers, mapping, branches) that transfer to every other tool. If you hit a wall, you will know exactly which wall, and that tells you whether you need n8n's code, Zapier's simplicity, or Gumloop's AI focus.

## The meta lesson

Tools change; concepts do not. Triggers, actions, mapping, branching, loops, and error handling appear in every automation platform under different names. Learn them once in Make and you can pick up any tool in a weekend. That is the real return on this guide.

## Try before you commit

All three tools have free tiers or trials. The fastest evaluation is a bake off: build the same simple automation in each one. A good test project is "when a form is submitted, enrich the data, and notify the team," because it exercises triggers, mapping, and branching. Time yourself in each tool and note where you got stuck. Your own experience beats any comparison article, including this one.

## Revisit yearly

The automation landscape moves fast. Pricing changes, features launch, and your needs evolve. A tool that was perfect at ten workflows might strain at fifty. Once a year, ask: are we fighting the tool? Are bills surprising us? Is there a category of automation we avoid because the tool makes it hard? Honest answers keep your stack matched to your reality.

## The skill that matters most

Whichever tool you pick, the durable skill is workflow thinking: breaking a messy process into triggers, steps, decisions, and outputs. That skill transfers across Make, n8n, Zapier, Gumloop, and whatever launches next year. Tools are rented; thinking is owned. Invest accordingly.
